title: Given an array of integers that may include positives and negatives, find the minimum sum obtainable from any contiguous non-empty subarray. Solve it with the minimum variant of Kadane's algorithm and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
shortTitle: Minimum Subarray Sum (Smallest Sum Contiguous Subarray, Kadane's Minimum Variant)

s1_definition.profdef: The minimum subarray sum problem asks for the smallest possible sum of any contiguous non-empty subarray of an integer array. It is solved with the mirror image of Kadane's algorithm: at each position we compute the minimum sum of a subarray ending exactly there, which is either the current element alone or the current element added to the minimum sum ending at the previous position, whichever is smaller, while tracking the global minimum of those local values. It runs in a single linear pass.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh reviews a sequence of daily net cash movements for an account, deposits as positives and withdrawals as negatives, and wants the worst continuous drawdown, the stretch of consecutive days that drained the most cash. As he walks day by day he asks whether his running decline is still getting worse by continuing, or whether he should abandon it and start a fresh decline from today, always remembering the deepest decline he has ever recorded.
s1_definition.oneliner: At each element, either extend the running minimum or restart from this element, and keep the smallest running sum ever seen.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The minimum subarray sum problem asks for the smallest possible sum of any contiguous non-empty subarray of an integer array. It is solved with the mirror image of Kadane's algorithm: at each position we compute the minimum sum of a subarray ending exactly there, which is either the current element alone or the current element added to the minimum sum ending at the previous position, whichever is smaller, while tracking the global minimum of those local values. It runs in a single linear pass.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh reviews a sequence of daily net cash movements for an account, deposits as positives and withdrawals as negatives, and wants the worst continuous drawdown, the stretch of consecutive days that drained the most cash. As he walks day by day he asks whether his running decline is still getting worse by continuing, or whether he should abandon it and start a fresh decline from today, always remembering the deepest decline he has ever recorded.

**One line to remember:** At each element, either extend the running minimum or restart from this element, and keep the smallest running sum ever seen.

sections.s2_technical:
The minimum subarray sum is the exact mirror of the maximum version, and the same dynamic-programming insight applies: the minimum subarray must end somewhere, so if we compute the minimum sum of a subarray ending at each position, the overall answer is the smallest of those. This turns a search over all start and end pairs into one linear scan.

We keep a current minimum, the smallest sum of a subarray ending at the current index, and a global minimum, the best answer seen. For each element we update with `currentMin = Math.min(nums[i], currentMin + nums[i])`. This encodes the decision: either the best subarray ending here is just the element, which is chosen when the previous running sum was positive and therefore pulling us up away from the minimum, or it is the previous running minimum extended by this element. After updating, we refresh the global minimum with `globalMin = Math.min(globalMin, currentMin)`.

Initialization is the same careful point as in the maximum version but mirrored. Because the subarray must be non-empty and the array could be all positives, we seed both variables from the first element, `currentMin = globalMin = nums[0]`, and iterate from the second. Seeding the global minimum at zero would wrongly report zero for an all-positive array, when the correct answer is the single smallest element. The senior-level nuance is recognizing that minimum Kadane is not a separate algorithm to memorize but the same recurrence with the comparison direction flipped.

A clean alternative that senior engineers often mention is to negate every element, run the standard maximum Kadane, and negate the result, which reuses one implementation for both problems. If we need the indices of the worst stretch we track a tentative start that resets on restart and commit the best start and end when the global minimum improves. The time complexity is linear, O(n), and the space complexity is O(1). This mirror technique shows an interviewer that you understand the structure of Kadane's recurrence rather than just a single memorized form.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the liquidity-risk team reviews a sequence of daily net cash movements for a treasury account, where deposits are positive and withdrawals are negative. They need to identify the worst continuous drawdown, the consecutive run of days whose net movement was the most negative, along with its start and end, because that worst drawdown feeds the stress-testing model and sets intraday liquidity buffers. This is exactly the minimum subarray sum problem, where a deep negative run is the thing we are hunting for.

Problem 2 — Examining every possible run of days by brute force is quadratic and does not scale across the bank's treasury accounts and long histories. The minimum variant of Kadane's algorithm gives a single linear pass per account and yields the drawdown's date range directly, which makes the nightly stress-input computation practical.

The code has the shared `Account` class, a reused `StreakResult` style holder named `DrawdownResult`, a `DrawdownAnalyzer` service with a `worstDrawdown` method implementing minimum Kadane with index tracking, and a runnable `MinSubarraySumKadaneDemo` main class that runs Rajesh's and Priya's cash-movement sequences, logging restarts at fine level and the worst drawdown at info level.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's cash moves are 30, -40, -60, 20, -10, 50, -30. We seed the current minimum and global minimum both at the first element, 30, with starts at 0.

Step 1 at index 1, value -40: the current minimum 30 is positive, so we restart; current minimum becomes -40, tentative start becomes 1. Minus 40 is less than 30, so global minimum becomes -40, best start 1, best end 1.

Step 2 at index 2, value -60: current minimum -40 is not positive, so we extend; current minimum becomes -100. Minus 100 is less than -40, global minimum becomes -100, best start 1, best end 2.

Step 3 at index 3, value 20: current minimum -100 is not positive, extend; current minimum becomes -80. Global minimum stays -100.

Step 4 at index 4, value -10: extend; current minimum becomes -90. Global minimum stays -100.

Step 5 at index 5, value 50: extend; current minimum becomes -40. Global minimum stays -100.

Step 6 at index 6, value -30: current minimum -40 is not positive, extend; current minimum becomes -70. Global minimum stays -100.

The worst drawdown is -100, spanning days 1 through 2, the run -40 followed by -60.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The minimum subarray sum problem asks for the smallest sum of any contiguous non-empty subarray, and I solve it with the mirror image of Kadane's algorithm in a single linear pass. The same insight carries over: the minimum subarray ends somewhere, so if I compute the minimum sum of a subarray ending at each position, the answer is the smallest of those. I keep a running current minimum and a global minimum, and at each element I either extend the running minimum by this element or restart from this element alone, choosing whichever is smaller, then I update the global minimum.

The point I emphasize is that this is not a new algorithm to memorize but the same recurrence with the comparison direction flipped. I seed both variables from the first element and iterate from the second, because the array might be all positive, in which case the correct answer is the single smallest element rather than zero. I also mention the clean shortcut of negating every element, running standard maximum Kadane, and negating the result, which reuses one implementation for both the maximum and minimum problems and signals that I understand the symmetry.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on the liquidity-risk team. Daily net cash movements for a treasury account arrived as signed amounts, deposits positive and withdrawals negative, and we needed the worst continuous drawdown, the consecutive run whose net movement was the most negative, along with its date range, because that fed the stress-testing model and set intraday liquidity buffers. I tracked a tentative start that reset on each restart and committed the best range when the global minimum improved, so the output was the reportable drawdown window, and the linear pass scaled across all treasury accounts.

The senior-level point I make is that recognizing minimum Kadane as the maximum recurrence with a flipped comparison, or equivalently as maximum Kadane over negated inputs, demonstrates that I grasp the structure rather than a single memorized form. I also note the identical seeding pitfall around the all-positive case, and that for monetary values I accumulate in a long or BigDecimal to prevent overflow across long histories. Showing the symmetry, the shared pitfall, and the production-grade numeric handling is what distinguishes a candidate who truly owns the technique.
